title: The Legend of Zelda: Phantom Hourglass

nodes.name: Stylus input, steering and gesture recognition
nodes.purpose: Samples the touchscreen, maps the stylus to a world-plane offset, decides tap and hold goals, and turns strokes into sword swings and aim points.

nodes.name: Player state handlers, interaction and equipment
nodes.purpose: Holds the character state machine: movement, damage reactions, grabbing, pushing, throwing, and the hammer charge and swing timing.

nodes.name: Actor bodies, gravity and floor contact
nodes.purpose: Base actor with position, velocity, gravity, fall cap, cylinder hitbox, floor snapping and a near or far activity class.

nodes.name: Combat contact, shield and damage reactions
nodes.purpose: Resolves sword, shield, hammer and roll contacts, picks a reaction level per incoming object, and applies knockback, damage windows and respawn.

nodes.name: Map grid, floor heights and room camera viewpoints
nodes.purpose: Serves the one-unit tile grid, per-tile floor heights and the authored camera viewpoint table used to frame each room.

cards.name: Stylus position to world-plane offset
cards.summary: The stylus position is mapped to a world offset from the screen centre, and a small radius around the character is ignored.
cards.behavior: Steering uses the stylus, not an analogue stick. The last stylus position is converted into a world-space offset: the horizontal distance from the screen centre at 128 pixels and the vertical distance from the centre at 96 pixels are scaled so that the full screen width and the full screen height each cover 10.625 world units. The result is a point on a horizontal plane at the character, with the screen vertical axis becoming world depth. Because the screen is wider than it is tall, one pixel sideways is a smaller world step than one pixel up or down; the reach is about 0.04 world units per pixel across and 0.06 per pixel down. Stylus distance from the character under 20 pixels is treated as no input, so a small accidental drift does not move the character. The same plane is used for movement goals, aim points and the fairy follow point, so all stylus-driven behaviour shares one mapping.

constants.name: Horizontal centre of the touchscreen
constants.unit: pixels from the left edge, sampled per update, rate unverified

constants.name: Vertical centre of the touchscreen
constants.unit: pixels from the top edge, sampled per update, rate unverified

constants.name: World span of the full screen width and height
constants.unit: world units across 256 pixels horizontally and across 192 pixels vertically, static mapping with no timestep

constants.name: Stylus dead zone around the character
constants.unit: pixels of stylus offset, sampled per update, rate unverified

cards.name: Stylus distance to movement-speed fraction
cards.summary: Speed is the square of stylus distance over an 80-pixel reference, softened during the first four updates of a contact.
cards.behavior: The character has a continuous speed fraction rather than a fixed walk. The engine divides the stylus distance from the character by 80 pixels and squares the quotient, so half the reference distance yields a quarter of the speed, three quarters of the reference yields about 56 percent, and only a stylus at or beyond 80 pixels yields the full walk speed. While a contact is younger than four updates the fraction is reduced by a quarter for each update still missing, so tapping far from the character does not start at full speed. The fraction is clamped between zero and one. With no contact the fraction is zero, unless a held button flag is present, in which case the full value is returned. The squaring means most of the usable speed range sits in the outer half of the reference radius, which keeps small stylus wobble from producing large speed changes.

constants.name: Reference stylus distance for full speed
constants.unit: pixels between stylus and character, sampled per update, rate unverified

constants.name: Ramp length at the start of a contact
constants.unit: updates of the touch state machine, rate unverified

constants.name: Upper clamp of the speed fraction
constants.unit: dimensionless fraction of the walk speed, recomputed per update, rate unverified

cards.name: Tap and short hold to approach
cards.summary: A contact that ends within 21 updates and 10 pixels of where the drag started selects a goal, and 15 updates without progress drops it.
cards.behavior: A tap is a contact that ends within 21 updates of starting, provided the release point is within 10 pixels of the point where the drag was recorded. On a tap the engine first looks for an object under the stylus and otherwise uses the map point under the stylus. That target becomes a follow goal and the character walks toward it without further input. A separate hold rule accepts a contact of 15 to 29 updates on the same object and returns that object as the interaction target when the direct follow reference is gone, which is how holding an object keeps the character working on it. While following a map point, the distance to the goal is compared with the previous update; progress of 0.01 world units or less counts as stuck, and 15 stuck updates cancel the follow. Touching down again cancels an existing follow immediately, and the end of a cutscene arms a 15-update delay before a tap is accepted.

constants.unit: updates of the touch state machine, rate unverified

constants.name: Squared tap radius around the drag start
constants.unit: square pixels, equal to a 10-pixel radius, checked once on release, no timestep

constants.name: Follow progress below which the character counts as stuck
constants.unit: world units of distance change per update, rate unverified

constants.name: Stuck updates before a follow order is dropped

cards.name: Nearest touchable body under the stylus
cards.summary: The stylus selects the nearest living actor whose projected hitbox covers the touch point, not the first match in the actor table.
cards.behavior: Structured touch input needs to know which body the player meant. Selection scans the whole actor table and keeps the closest qualifying hit rather than stopping at the first. A candidate qualifies when it is alive, carries a non-zero interaction class, is marked touchable by the actor or by the current mode, and has its hitbox projected over the stylus position. Distance is measured in three dimensions from the character, so a small body under the stylus beats a large body further away even when both overlap the touch point. The projection lifts the hitbox centre by its own radius and uses that radius as the on-screen tolerance, so tall bodies are easier to hit near their top. The same rule runs when the stylus is released, which is why tapping between two overlapping objects picks the closer one.

cards.name: Stylus stroke to sword swing class
cards.summary: A stroke must travel 10 pixels, and its direction against the facing picks one of four swing classes; fast strokes take a side class directly.
cards.behavior: Attacks are recognised from the shape of a stylus stroke on release. The stroke is accepted when the contact lasted fewer than 21 updates, or when the fast part of the contact arrived and the slow part lasted longer than 21 updates. The stroke must cover at least 10 pixels; when the alternate touch context applies the minimum rises to 20 pixels. If stylus travel speed is above 0.5 pixels per update the attack takes the fast variant and the side of the stroke relative to the stroke angle chooses the left or right class. Otherwise the stroke direction is compared with the facing recorded at the start of the drag: more than 135 degrees to either side gives class 0, 45 to 135 degrees gives class 1, minus 45 to minus 135 degrees gives class 2, and within 45 degrees gives class 3. When the stylus stayed within 10 pixels of the character, the attack uses the angle from the start of the drag and skips the side selection.

cards.name: Aim point for boomerang, bow, hammer and rope
cards.summary: A held stylus produces a world aim point capped at 4 units, with an 8-unit reach for longer items and a 4.2-unit fairy height.
cards.behavior: Directional items do not turn the character toward an attack; they read an aim. Two forms exist. The short aim vector, used by the boomerang, the bow and the rope, starts updating after the stylus has been held for 16 updates: the screen-centre offset becomes a direction whose length is clamped to 4 world units, so a stylus at the screen edge cannot aim arbitrarily far. When the stylus sits closer than 24 pixels to the character, the short aim collapses onto the character instead of pointing somewhere behind it. The long aim point, used by the hammer, is built from the same projected plane but measured from the character and clamped to 8 world units, and it is kept when the stylus lifts so the item does not snap back at the end of a stroke. A fairy follow point derived from the same plane sits 4.2 world units above the touch point.

constants.unit: updates of the touch state machine, rate unverified

constants.name: Aim direction length cap
constants.unit: world units from the character, recomputed per update while the stylus is held, rate unverified

constants.name: Aim reach for long items

constants.name: Fairy follow height above the stylus plane
constants.unit: world units above the touch point, sampled per update, rate unverified

cards.name: Gravity, fall cap and floor snap
cards.summary: Actors accelerate downward by 0.0498 units per update, cap their fall at 0.5 units per update, then snap up to the map floor.
cards.behavior: Falling is integrated once per actor update: vertical velocity loses 0.0498 world units per update and the downward speed is clamped at 0.5 world units per update. From rest the cap is reached in about ten updates, so a fall settles into a constant descent quickly instead of accelerating without bound. The floor snap runs separately from gravity: the map floor height under the actor is sampled using both the current and the previous position, and the actor is lifted to that height when it has passed below it. Because the height query receives the higher of the two positions, a fast descent is still caught at the floor rather than passing through a step. Each actor owns its gravity and fall cap, so a flying or floating body only has to change those two values instead of switching to a separate physics mode.

constants.name: Default downward acceleration
constants.unit: world units per update squared, rate unverified

constants.name: Default fall speed cap
constants.unit: world units per update, rate unverified

cards.name: Cylinder bodies and contact reach
cards.summary: Bodies are upright cylinders whose single size value is radius and height, half a world unit by default, against a one-unit player radius.
cards.behavior: Collision bodies are upright cylinders. One size value serves as both radius and height, a negative size disables the body entirely so that visual-only effects never collide, and the body can be offset from its owner origin and is rotated with the owner facing before overlap tests. A newly spawned actor starts with a body of 0.5 world units. Contact reach is measured from the player centre to the actor centre against the sum of the actor body radius and the player body radius, which is fixed at 1.0 world unit. That is why a large body can be struck from further away than a small one and why the player counts as a wider target than a default enemy.

constants.name: Default actor body size
constants.unit: world units, used as both radius and height, set once at spawn, no timestep

constants.name: Player body radius used in contact reach
constants.unit: world units added to the actor radius, evaluated once per contact, no timestep

cards.name: Near and far actor classification
cards.summary: An actor within 10 units of the player on both horizontal axes is classed near, everything else far, unless it carries a pending flag.
cards.behavior: Actor activity is classified from distance instead of a streaming grid. The engine measures the absolute difference on the horizontal axes between the player and the actor; an actor within 10 world units on both axes counts as near, and anything beyond either limit counts as far. An actor with any of several pending flags set, including being grabbed or carrying an interaction highlight, is forced into the active class regardless of distance, so an object the player is carrying keeps updating. The routine only assigns the class; it does not move or delete the actor. The result is a cheap square instead of a circle, which means a body just inside the diagonal corner is still near and the cost is two absolute differences and two comparisons per actor.

constants.name: Near radius on each horizontal axis
constants.unit: world units from the player, evaluated per classification pass, rate unverified

cards.name: Shield arc and contact priority
cards.summary: The shield covers 90 degrees each side of the facing, and contacts resolve in the order sword, shield, hammer, roll.
cards.behavior: A block is angle based. The engine measures the angle between the player facing and the direction to the attacking body, and the shield can only block when that angle is at most 90 degrees, so the guard covers the whole front half and nothing beside or behind the player. The shield volume must also overlap the incoming body. Contact resolution is a fixed chain: sword overlap is tested first, then the shield, then the hammer, then the Goron roll, and the first branch that matches produces the reaction and stops the chain. Each branch fills its own reaction record, so one body never receives two reactions in the same update, and the sword hit wins when the sword and the shield both overlap. A blocked contact carries a different reaction from a sword hit, and an upgraded wisdom fairy raises the blocked reaction by one step.

constants.name: Shield half-angle around the facing
constants.unit: degrees, evaluated once per contact, no timestep

constants.name: Wisdom fairy level that upgrades a block reaction
constants.unit: fairy level, dimensionless, checked once per contact, no timestep

cards.name: Hit reaction level per incoming object
cards.summary: Each projectile or carried object maps to a fixed reaction level, from 1 for a sword beam to 11 for an unknown source.
cards.behavior: When an object strikes a body, the reaction is chosen from the identity of the source rather than from its speed or mass. A sword beam produces level 1, an arrow level 7, a boomerang level 5, a grappling hook level 8, and the bomb family, blasts and bombchus level 6. A group of nine heavy or carried object ids, including the big rock, the stone, the barrel, the pot, the flying pot, the boss key and the force gem, produces level 10. One further source id produces level 4 and anything unlisted falls back to level 11. For arrows and sword beams the knockback direction is built from the facing of the shooter, while other sources use the difference between the body position and the previous position of the source, so a rolling object pushes away from where it came from.

constants.unit: reaction index used to pick a hit animation, dimensionless; per hit, no timestep

cards.name: Knockback, damage window and respawn
cards.summary: A hit writes the knockback vector straight into player velocity, turns the body away from the blow, and respawns after a 0.6-unit lift.
cards.behavior: Damage does not blend with movement. The incoming knockback vector is written directly into player velocity, the damage state index is set, and the facing is replaced by the direction of the blow plus half a turn, leaving the body with its back to the source. The damage state also stores the reaction level used to choose the animation. Minor damage plays over a 10-frame window at 1.5 times speed, with the start and end frames taken from the midpoint of the character animation length, and the front and back variants are tuned separately. Death does not drop the body at once: the player is lifted 0.6 world units above its position, a respawn callback runs when the lift completes, and the body is displaced by the offset stored around the last jump. Health is clamped between zero and the current maximum whenever it is set or added, so healing cannot exceed the cap and damage cannot go negative.

constants.name: Minor damage animation end frame
constants.unit: q20.12 fixed point, equal to 10 animation frames, rate unverified

constants.name: Minor damage playback speed
constants.unit: q20.12 fixed point, equal to 1.5 times playback speed, per update, rate unverified

constants.name: Lift applied before the respawn callback
constants.unit: q20.12 fixed point world units, equal to 0.6 world units, applied once on death, no timestep

constants.name: Facing flip applied on knockback
constants.unit: binary angle units, half a turn of 65536 units per full turn, applied once per hit, no timestep

cards.name: Grab, push and throw an object
cards.summary: Pushing is capped at one twelfth of a world unit per update and a throw leaves at 0.16 times the throw strength along the aim.
cards.behavior: Object interaction is a state machine over approach, push, lift, carry and throw. While pushing, the player planar velocity is rebuilt from the object position so that each axis contributes at most one twelfth of a world unit per update, and the forward term is shortened by the object body size plus 0.4 world units so the player pushes against the body rather than into it. Melee targeting during interaction uses reach of the object radius plus 3.5 world units, then narrows to a close band under 1.8 units, a mid band under 2.7 units with a 1.2-unit vertical tolerance, and a far band used only when a separate state flag is clear. Lifting uses 1.6 speed and its animation window ends at frame 10; throwing uses 1.0 speed and ends at frame 15. A two-update stop time is armed when a push or pull starts. A thrown object leaves along the aim at 0.16 times the throw strength. When a bomb-type item is equipped, the toss offset becomes 0.3 world units along the facing instead of the stylus-derived offset, and one helper refuses to launch a carried object unless it is a bomb or a cucco.

constants.unit: divisor of one world unit per update, so the push cap is 1/12 world unit per update, rate unverified

constants.name: Melee reach beyond the object body

constants.name: Throw speed per unit of throw strength
constants.unit: world units per update per strength unit, rate unverified

constants.name: Pickup throw offset

constants.name: Lift animation speed
constants.unit: q20.12 fixed point, equal to 1.6 times playback speed, per update, rate unverified

constants.unit: updates of the interaction state, rate unverified

cards.name: Hammer charge, animation timing and aim turn
cards.summary: Holding the hammer charges for 40 updates, a swing locks the item for four updates, and the body turns toward the aim in 45-degree steps.
cards.behavior: The hammer is held to charge. Holding the touch input starts a charge timer, the item state moves from idle to charging and then to charged when 40 updates have passed; releasing earlier still swings, but without the charged state. After a swing the item is locked for four updates so a new charge cannot start immediately. The release point is the aimed world position taken from the long stylus aim, and each release hands that point to the map. Four hammer animation records exist: a 64-frame entry clip at speed 1.0, mid clips of 5 and 3 frames at 1.0, and a 6-frame clip at 1.2 used while the charge is held. While a hammer action is pending the player turns toward the stored impact point with a step capped at 45 degrees per update, which lets a slow aim correction look like a deliberate wind-up rather than an instant snap.

cards.name: Hammer ground strike over nine tiles
cards.summary: A hammer release scans the impact tile and its eight neighbours, skipping map edges and floors that differ too much from the player height.
cards.behavior: A hammer release hands the impact position to the map, and the map scans a three-by-three block of tiles centred on the tile under that position. Candidate coordinates outside the map width or height are skipped, so an impact at the edge of a room scans only the tiles that exist. Before a tile can trigger, the ground height at the centre tile is compared with the player height and the difference must be below a small tolerance, which keeps an impact from reaching objects on a floor above or below. The scan keeps the last object id returned by a qualifying tile and reports a miss when none qualifies. Because the area is a square of tiles rather than a radius, the strike covers the same number of tiles wherever inside the centre tile the hammer lands, and the coverage never becomes a circle.

constants.name: Tiles scanned beyond the impact tile on each axis
constants.unit: tiles on each side, giving a 3 by 3 block per strike, no timestep

cards.name: Per-room camera viewpoints
cards.summary: Each map ships a viewpoint table, and a per-slot id selects one, falling back to a mode default when the id is zero or missing.
cards.behavior: Camera framing is authored with the map rather than computed from the player. A map owns a table of viewpoints, and each entry stores a position, a pair of identifiers and four scalar parameters. Two independent slots hold a current viewpoint id, so two consumers can select different entries from the same table at the same time. A slot id of zero, or an id that does not occur in the table, does not leave the camera undefined: the map supplies a default id instead, which is 28 for most of the alternate-mode cases and zero otherwise. Selecting a viewpoint copies the whole record into the caller structure, so switching rooms only swaps entries instead of rebuilding the map. Because the table is data-driven, a room can cut to a new angle without any player-relative camera logic running.

constants.name: Viewpoint slots held per map
constants.unit: independent viewpoint ids, one per view; no timestep

constants.name: Alternate default viewpoint id
constants.unit: viewpoint table id, decimal 28, chosen when the slot id is unset or missing, no timestep

cards.name: One-unit tile grid and per-tile floor height
cards.summary: Tile starts are offset plus index times 4096 in fixed point, so tiles are one world unit; a tile box begins 1.2 units below its floor.
cards.behavior: Map geometry is queried on a square tile grid. A tile start is the map offset plus the tile index times 4096 in fixed point, the tile end adds the same step, so a tile is exactly one world unit on each horizontal axis. Tile-based positions are centred by adding half a unit to the start on both axes, which is the point used for floor sampling and for tile targeting. The box used for tile tests begins 1.2 world units below the floor and ends at the tile stored floor height, so a character standing on the tile is inside its box even when the floor is above the character origin. Because everything is fixed point, a tile offset can be added straight to a world coordinate with no conversion, so a tile lookup costs a multiply and two adds.

constants.name: Tile size
constants.unit: q20.12 fixed point world units, equal to 1.0 world unit per tile on each horizontal axis, static geometry with no timestep

constants.name: Tile centre offset
constants.unit: q20.12 fixed point world units, equal to 0.5 world units from the tile start, static offset with no timestep

constants.name: Tile box floor margin
constants.unit: world units below the tile floor, applied when a tile box is built, no timestep
